brief.head: Lazy typists’ word
brief.text: Computer sci­ence once ran in English on 127 ASCII char­ac­ters, Ajay Shah said. To sup­port other lan­guages, lazy typ­ists short­ened in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion to I18N: I, 18 let­ters, N. {048-J07}

brief.head: Exports on paper
brief.text: Subsidies like PLI, or a rupee pushed to 100 a dol­lar, can pro­duce ex­ports with­out pro­duc­tiv­ity. That, Shah said, mixes up means and ends. {048-C06}

brief.head: Patriots compete
brief.text: Borrowing a dis­tinc­tion from Ram Guha, Amit Varma called pa­tri­o­tism love of coun­try, and na­tion­al­ism toxic and chest-thumping. A true pa­triot, he said, wants India to com­pete. {048-C15}

brief.head: Dwarfs by design
brief.text: India’s quirky rules, from SEBI and RBI reg­u­la­tions to UPI, shape firms whose sys­tems are use­less abroad. Policymakers, Shah warned, are “cre­at­ing dwarfs”. {048-C14}

brief.head: China’s loss, not ours
brief.text: Global firms found them­selves too ex­posed to China and rushed to di­ver­sify. “Sadly, not much has hap­pened in terms of Indian gains out of this process,” Shah said. {048-J13}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on why Indian firms must face the world
lead.head: Made in India, tested abroad

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 48

body: Every coun­try has labour, Ajay Shah said. The puz­zle of de­vel­op­ment is get­ting that labour to do more in each work­ing hour, and that hap­pens, by and large, in­side firms.
“So get­ting to high pro­duc­tiv­ity firms is the nec­es­sary and suf­fi­cient con­di­tion of be­com­ing an ad­vanced econ­omy,” he told Amit Varma. {048-C01}
If a quar­ter of Indians were pro­duc­ing at the pro­duc­tiv­ity of first world coun­tries, Shah said, “we are done”. Only a third of work­ing-age Indians work today, he added.

The episode took its title, *Graduating to Globalisation*, from one of Shah’s pa­pers. Its sub­ject was how Indian firms reach the fron­tier: through in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion, which com­puter sci­en­tists shorten to I18N.
## More than ex­ports
A firm can be­come con­nected to the world in many ways, Shah said. It can im­port spe­cialised in­puts, ex­port, raise for­eign eq­uity and debt, hire for­eign­ers and build op­er­a­tions abroad.
Policy econ­o­mists, he com­plained, treat these as a menu, pick­ing some and re­ject­ing oth­ers. In his view they feed one an­other, and a push on one helps the rest.
Exporting mat­ters most, but not for the rea­son busi­ness peo­ple think. When a whole coun­try ex­ports more, its cur­rency rises and cheaper im­ports kill off some do­mes­tic pro­duc­ers.
“The game is not to get rev­enues out of ex­ports,” Shah said. “The im­por­tant point is ex­port­ing is pass­ing a mar­ket test.” {048-C04}
A firm that can sell abroad, he said, has proved it is world class.

Exporting also cleans up pol­i­tics. At home, firms com­pete by turn­ing a weak state on one an­other, through favourable reg­u­la­tions, tax raids and joint lob­by­ing to keep for­eign­ers out. No amount of lob­by­ing in Delhi helps Infosys sell to Germany. {048-C05}
## Out of the way
The same logic em­braces multi­na­tion­als. About half of global trade hap­pens within firms, Shah said, so a coun­try can­not love ex­ports and dis­like multi­na­tion­als.

Firms will still ask for sub­si­dies: PLI, free land, re­lief from costly elec­tric­ity. Every lo­ca­tion has cheap and dear in­puts, Shah said; let firms choose. “So we should just kick the firms out of the room when they want a sub­sidy.” {048-C10}
Varma no­ticed that most of what Shah asked of the state was to get out of the way. “We are in­no­va­tive, we are cre­ative, we are en­tre­pre­neur­ial,” Varma said. “We’ll take care of shit.”
For man­agers, Shah posed a ques­tion: is your skill fix­ing the Indian sys­tem, or being a com­pe­tent firm? If the lat­ter, look out­side, where the mar­ket is in­fi­nite.
Boards and in­vestors, he said, can use in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion as a test that is very hard to fake.
## A plea to re­searchers

Shah closed with a plea to re­searchers. If de­vel­op­ment eco­nom­ics is about poverty pro­grammes and re­dis­tri­bu­tion, he said, it is at the wrong end of the puz­zle and in­creas­ingly ir­rel­e­vant to India’s jour­ney.

The ques­tions that mat­ter, about firm pro­duc­tiv­ity and in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion, can­not be an­swered by ran­domised con­trolled tri­als, and Shah said he proudly works on them any­way. {048-C02}
Varma piled on. He would not be sur­prised, he said, by a trial some­where ask­ing whether peo­ple see a yel­low shirt as brighter than a black one.

second.label: Talent without borders
second.head: Wanted: a foreign boss
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why hiring should ignore nationality, right up to the top

pic.caption: Sundar Pichai in 2023
pic.credit: grapher: Lukasz Kobus (European Commission), CC BY 4.0

body: Sundar Pichai, an Indian im­mi­grant who be­came chief ex­ec­u­tive of Google, once said it would be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi im­mi­grant be­came chief ex­ec­u­tive of Infosys. Ajay Shah re­called the re­mark. {048-S03}

India is not ready, Shah said. People would cul­tur­ally re­sent a for­eigner run­ning well-loved com­pa­nies like Infosys or TCS. In America, Satya Nadella at Microsoft and Pichai at Google were or­di­nary ap­point­ments: “Nobody starts shout­ing anti-foreigner.”

Amit Varma turned it around: so many American com­pa­nies hav­ing Indian CEOs “speaks to the great­ness of America, not India”. For Shah, the loy­alty is to build­ing the firm, what­ever the na­tion­al­ity of the per­son hired.

quote.text: You should hire with­out re­gard to na­tion­al­ity.

third.head: The elephant in the mill

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Mr. Capital and the steel mill

body: An en­gi­neer sees a steel mill as iron ore from Orissa and Goa, an­thracite from Australia and im­ported ma­chines, Ajay Shah said.

An econ­o­mist sees the ele­phant in the room: cap­i­tal. Its cost per ton of steel is higher than ore, coal or labour. “Mr. Capital is the most im­por­tant input provider to make a prof­itable steel mill,” he said. {#mrcapital}
To match the best mills in Korea, Japan or America, an Indian mill needs their cost of cap­i­tal. Foreign eq­uity and debt are cheaper, partly be­cause India is poor and its fi­nan­cial sys­tem bad.

So in­ter­fer­ing with ac­cess to for­eign cap­i­tal, Shah said, is as silly as in­ter­fer­ing with ac­cess to im­ported coal. {048-C08} Amit Varma told lis­ten­ers that in an ear­lier episode they had met Mr. Gas; today they had met Mr. Capital. {048-J04}

quote.text: So the jour­ney of de­vel­op­ment is the jour­ney of the emer­gence of high pro­duc­tiv­ity firms.

box.title: The paper behind the title
box.text: The episode takes its name from *Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals*, by Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah. It stud­ies out­bound in­vest­ment: Indian com­pa­nies build­ing fac­to­ries and com­pa­nies abroad, which Shah said hun­dreds now do. {#outbound}

sections.label: The starting point
sections.head: Where productivity lives
sections.caption: why firms matter
body: Amit Varma opened by plac­ing the episode in a longer body of work on firms, after ear­lier episodes on fam­ily firms and on the move from im­pe­rial to adap­tive firms. {048-R20} He called Ajay Shah’s think­ing on the sub­ject novel, a kind of schol­ar­ship that should be com­mon­place in the best uni­ver­si­ties.

Shah said his in­ter­est in firms comes from the grand­est ques­tion about India: can it be­come an ad­vanced econ­omy, with high per capita GDP, high lev­els of free­dom, and peo­ple “blos­som­ing into truth and beauty”?
## From first prin­ci­ples

Reasoning from first prin­ci­ples, he said, firms bub­ble into view. A firm is a coali­tion of cap­i­tal, man­agers, gov­er­nance, tech­nol­ogy and con­tracts, all meant to come to­gether to achieve high pro­duc­tiv­ity.

Gas money is not the same thing. Saudi Arabia and Qatar have high in­comes, Shah said, but pulling gas out of the ground does not build the firms, the knowl­edge or a changed so­ci­ety. Real de­vel­op­ment is “a human story”. {048-C01}

That story, he ar­gued, has a moral edge. The econ­o­mist George Stigler taught that a cap­i­tal­ist who dis­crim­i­nates against a cho­sen mi­nor­ity is harm­ing her­self, so suc­cess­ful firms are mer­i­to­cratic. {#stigler}
~ The task, Shah said, is to ask what makes firms like ASML, TSMC and Sony work so well, and why India does not cre­ate firms like them. {048-J12}

quote.text: So the jour­ney of de­vel­op­ment is the jour­ney of the emer­gence of high pro­duc­tiv­ity firms.

art.caption: Ajay Shah on why firms matter

sections.label: The modes
sections.head: Six doors to the world
sections.caption: the modes of internationalisation
body: Firm in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion, Ajay Shah said, is the broad idea that a firm be­comes deeply con­nected to the globe. His key claim: it is good for pro­duc­tiv­ity, and India grows bet­ter firms by em­pha­sis­ing it.

The first mode is im­ports. Local in­puts are usu­ally cheaper and eas­ier, Shah said, so im­ports tend to be highly spe­cialised tech­nol­ogy, ma­chines and ser­vices that firms go to real trou­ble to get. {#wanton}
Then come ex­ports, and then for­eign cap­i­tal: eq­uity, run­ning from port­fo­lio in­vest­ment to FDI, where in the limit a for­eign firm owns all of an Indian one, and debt bor­rowed abroad.
## Hiring and going out
Foreign em­ploy­ees bring spe­cialised knowl­edge, skills and re­la­tion­ships that can un­lock a mar­ket, Shah said, though hir­ing friends and fam­ily at home is eas­ier.

The last mode runs the other way. When an Indian com­pany builds a fac­tory or a com­pany abroad, Shah said, “that’s also a glo­ri­ous thing”. Hundreds of Indian firms now do it, the sub­ject of his paper *Graduating to Globalisation*. {#outbound}
~ Amit Varma, ask­ing how the modes fit to­gether, bor­rowed a fa­mous line: no man is an is­land, and no mode of I18N is an is­land ei­ther.

quote.text: On any of the six di­men­sions you push for­ward in one di­men­sion, it’ll end up help­ing the other di­men­sions.

sections.label: The market test
sections.head: Sell to Germany, not Delhi
sections.caption: why exporting is magic
body: Business peo­ple love ex­ports as extra sales, Ajay Shah said. But what is good for one com­pany does not scale to the econ­omy: that is a fal­lacy of com­po­si­tion.

When a coun­try suc­ceeds at ex­port­ing, its ex­change rate ap­pre­ci­ates and im­ports kill off some do­mes­tic pro­duc­ers. India’s soft­ware ex­ports pushed up the rupee and hurt man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports, which econ­o­mists call Dutch dis­ease. “That’s part of life,” Shah said. {048-J11}
Exporting also widens a firm’s mar­ket and brings economies of scale. For a global firm, size sig­nals qual­ity; for a local mo­nop­oly like Coal India, it means noth­ing.
## A cleaner game

Drawing on Jagdish Bhagwati, T. N. Srinivasan and Anne Krueger, Shah ar­gued that ex­port­ing changes a country’s po­lit­i­cal econ­omy. Infosys can­not lobby its way to German cus­tomers. Its only path is pro­duc­tiv­ity: “Like shut up and do your god­damn job bet­ter.” {048-J05}
There is a coun­ter­feit, though. Subsidies or a weak rupee, at 100 to the dol­lar in­stead of 80, can get even in­ef­fi­cient firms ex­port­ing. {#rupee}
~ Amit Varma made his rec­om­men­da­tion for the episode here: Bhagwati’s *In Defense of Globalization*, which he called a mag­nif­i­cent book that ev­ery­one should read. {048-R01}

quote.text: So even in a bad coun­try, pres­sure of ex­port­ing brings out bet­ter be­hav­ior from the firms.

sections.label: All of a piece
sections.head: No mode is an island
sections.caption: multinationals and foreign talent
body: Many pol­icy econ­o­mists treat the modes of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion as a menu of choices, Ajay Shah said. “Do I want this, do I not want this? He loves me, he loves me not.” {048-J06}
Modern trade the­ory says oth­er­wise. A full 50 per cent of global trade hap­pens within firms, and smart firms ig­nore bor­ders, look­ing for low costs and for di­ver­si­fi­ca­tion. {#fifty}
An en­gine is made in Brazil, as­sem­bled into a car in Madras, and the car is sold in America. So a coun­try that wants ex­ports must be all in on FDI, com­ing in and going out.

Shah had no time for George Fernandes, “ob­ses­sively ir­ri­tated about multi­na­tional cor­po­ra­tions op­er­at­ing in India”, or for the tax and rules-of-origin tor­ment the Indian state in­flicts on them. {048-J09}
## Blind to pass­ports

Hiring fol­lows the same logic. “The con­sid­er­a­tion of the na­tion­al­ity of the job ap­pli­cant should be deleted in the HR data­base at the point of ap­pli­ca­tion,” Shah said. Not hir­ing South Koreans is as wrong as not hir­ing Muslims or Dalits. {048-C09}
~ The modes re­in­force one an­other, he said. Foreign work­ers know cheap ven­dors back home; for­eign share­hold­ers and board mem­bers can open the door to FDI in Brazil.

quote.text: If you like ex­port­ing, you like multi­na­tion­als. These are one of a piece.

sections.label: For policymakers
sections.head: Smile, and let firms choose
sections.caption: subsidy-seekers and the state
body: Amit Varma turned to role play: I am a pol­icy per­son, what do I do? Ajay Shah’s an­swer was that firm pro­duc­tiv­ity, driven by in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion, is the heart and soul of India’s de­vel­op­ment jour­ney. Education and health are means to that end.

Firms will al­ways come ask­ing for help, he said: PLI, free land, cheaper elec­tric­ity. But every lo­ca­tion has its trade-offs. Labour costs more in Brazil than in India; elec­tric­ity costs less in Germany. The pol­i­cy­maker, he said, should smile at the firm and let it choose where and what to pro­duce.
India should fix its elec­tric­ity pol­icy, Shah said, but it is a 25-year jour­ney, and that does not jus­tify a sub­sidy. {#electricity}
A fac­tory with 20 work­ers burn­ing 20 megawatt hours a day prob­a­bly be­longs in Germany, he said. Firms that want sub­si­dies, he said, should be kicked out of the room. {048-C10}
## The anti-foreign re­flex

Then there is the state’s hos­til­ity to the out­side world. Foreign bank ac­counts, travel abroad, sub­sidiaries abroad and run­ning a busi­ness through Dubai are all treated as bad, across SEBI, RBI, the Enforcement Directorate, in­come tax and GST.
~ Smaller firms sim­ply give up, Shah said. In London you can open a bank ac­count within 10 min­utes; a for­eigner try­ing to do so in India suf­fers mis­ery. {048-C11}

quote.text: This is the Indian state harm­ing India’s jour­ney.

sections.label: For managers
sections.head: An infinite market awaits
sections.caption: managers, boards and investors
body: For man­agers, boards and in­vestors, Ajay Shah’s strate­gic idea was sim­ple: do more in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion. Every firm should ask whether its skill is fix­ing the Indian sys­tem or being a com­pe­tent firm. {048-C12}

A com­pe­tent firm should keep away from the Indian state, he said. Even a clean firm will find com­peti­tors hurl­ing the state at it. The world mar­ket is in­fi­nite, and a firm can keep grow­ing in it for 25 years.
## Hard to fake

Boards can use in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion to hold man­agers to ac­count be­yond quar­ter-to-quarter profit: ex­port share and growth, as­sets abroad, cheaper global cap­i­tal, for­eign hires, spe­cialised im­ports, the num­ber of coun­tries. Amit Varma called it a “fast and fru­gal heuris­tic”. {048-J15}

Shah ap­plied the test to a clas­si­fi­ca­tion by their friend Nitin Pai of India’s IT firms: ser­vices ex­porters like TCS and Wipro, soft­ware-as-a-service ex­porters, and do­mes­tic firms. The first two pass the mar­ket test. {#nitin}

~ Domestic win­ners need more scru­tiny. PayPal was blocked in India, Shah noted, and UPI now has a mo­nop­oly. “So is UPI ac­tu­ally good? Or did you do it through pro­tec­tion­ism? Who knows?” {#paypal}

quote.text: Those kinds of met­rics are very hard to fake, and they are deeply con­nected to firm pro­duc­tiv­ity.
What a true pa­triot will say is that no, that we have it in us to be as good as any­one in the world. Let us com­pete, we will get bet­ter, and we will show you what we can do.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Firecrackers, a stolen bridge, Korean conglomerates and India’s software heroes

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s breakfast story, and what it says about India
stories.head: Four floors, four bangs
body: At break­fast on the morn­ing of the record­ing, Amit Varma’s good friend Vaishnav told him a story from his school. Varma re­told it on air, ad­mit­ting he had for­got­ten some of the de­tails.

On a fes­ti­val day, which Varma thought might have been Diwali, a school­boy went up to the fifth floor of the build­ing. He car­ried some­thing he had made him­self: a chain, or a string, with fire­crack­ers at the end of it.
He had worked out a cun­ning way to set off a de­layed fire­cracker after 20 min­utes, and to time each one. {#fuse}
From the fifth floor he worked his ap­pa­ra­tus so that a fire­cracker dan­gled in the fourth-floor toi­let, an­other in the third-floor toi­let, and so on down to the first.
Then the fourth floor went off. All the teach­ers ran up to the fourth floor. When they got there, the third floor went off, and they ran down to it. Then the sec­ond went off.
Varma was not scan­dalised. “The first thought that came to my mind when Vaishnav told me the story is that these are the fu­ture of our coun­try,” he said. “This is in­no­va­tion.” {048-S01}
The boy was tak­ing the ini­tia­tive, Varma said, and doing some­thing funky in cre­ative ways. When such peo­ple get the op­por­tu­nity in the econ­omy, he said, they “can do amaz­ing things”.
~ Ajay Shah took up the thread: the task, he said, is to chan­nel that en­ergy into the in­sti­tu­tions called firms.
stories.why: Mischief and en­ter­prise draw on the same ini­tia­tive and cre­ativ­ity. Varma’s point was that India has such en­ergy in abun­dance and holds it back; Shah’s was that firms are where it can be put to pro­duc­tive use.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the schoolboy and the firecrackers

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Bihar, and the talent India wastes
stories.head: The bridge that wasn’t there
body: Amit Varma once recorded an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* about Bihar with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand, who told him about the in­cred­i­bly in­no­va­tive things hap­pen­ing there.
An en­tire bridge, for one, had been stolen. “People just stole a bridge. One day there was a bridge. It wasn’t there. Only in Bihar,” Varma said. {048-S02}
The bridge, he added, went only after a river had been stolen: a patch through which water ran. And many of the big tele­mar­ket­ing scams, he said, are run out of a cou­ple of towns in Bihar.

~ On one hand, Varma said, all this is bad. On the other, it shows India’s po­ten­tial: the imag­i­na­tion and the sheer num­bers to com­pete with any­body in the world. As a coun­try, he said, “we are con­strain­ing our­selves”.

quote.text: And the good part is in the po­ten­tial. This is a po­ten­tial our coun­try has.

stories.postscript: The show notes link a re­port of thieves steal­ing a 60-foot bridge in broad day­light, and an­other of a pond stolen in Bihar.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the stolen bridge

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells a favourite of Lant Pritchett’s
stories.head: Korea’s cosy deal, with a catch
body: The econ­o­mist Lant Pritchett, Ajay Shah said, al­ways pushes the story of South Korea’s chae­bols. In a way, you could call it crony cap­i­tal­ism, Shah con­ceded.
The gov­ern­ment struck a po­lit­i­cal bar­gain with eight or ten big busi­ness houses, promis­ing to cre­ate the con­di­tions in which they would ex­port. {#korea}

The beauty lay in the goal. There was noth­ing the Korean gov­ern­ment could do to make the American mar­ket more ac­ces­si­ble to a Korean man­u­fac­turer. It could not hurt an American com­pany, and pro­tec­tion­ism would not help. {048-S04}

~ So the whole lan­guage of the bar­gain be­came one of how to ex­port, and pub­lic pol­icy, Shah said, went in the cor­rect di­rec­tion: to­wards pro-social, pro-productivity, sen­si­ble ac­tiv­i­ties.
stories.why: A cosy bar­gain be­tween state and busi­ness can still raise pro­duc­tiv­ity when suc­cess is mea­sured in a mar­ket the state can­not rig. Exporting sup­plied that mea­sure, which is why, for Shah, it sits at the heart of de­vel­op­ment strat­egy.

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the heroes of Indian software
stories.head: They didn’t wait for the state
body: Better ed­u­ca­tion, health and elec­tric­ity pol­icy are all wel­come, Ajay Shah said. But each is a 25-year jour­ney, and in the short term none will move the nee­dle.

The he­roes of Indian soft­ware showed an­other way. TCS, Infosys and the rest did not wait for the gov­ern­ment to build en­gi­neer­ing col­leges where a mil­lion peo­ple a year would learn pro­gram­ming. “They just went ahead and solved their own prob­lems,” Shah said. {048-S05}
Their play­book, he said later, was min­i­mum in­ter­faces with the Indian state: com­pete abroad, and do not visit gov­ern­ment of­fices ask­ing for this favour and that. {048-C12}
~ There is enough op­por­tu­nity, en­ergy and hunger in India, Shah ar­gued, to make tremen­dous progress with­out wait­ing for all those things to be fixed.
stories.why: Waiting for the Indian state to fix elec­tric­ity, Shah said, is not going to hap­pen. India’s soft­ware firms showed the al­ter­na­tive: a can-do at­ti­tude, a world mar­ket and as lit­tle deal­ing with the gov­ern­ment as pos­si­ble.

quiz.a: It is a mar­ket test: a firm that ex­ports has proved it is world class.

quiz.a: The day a Bangladeshi im­mi­grant be­comes the chief ex­ec­u­tive of Infosys.

quiz.q: Which input to a steel mill does Shah say engineers overlook, though it costs most?
quiz.a: Capital, or Mr. Capital: its cost per ton ex­ceeds ore, coal and labour.

quiz.q: How did Amit Varma, following Ram Guha, tell patriotism from nationalism?
quiz.a: Patriotism is lov­ing your coun­try; na­tion­al­ism is toxic, ex­clu­sion­ary and chest-thumping.

quiz.q: Which four countries does Shah call the world’s great development experiences?
quiz.a: Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile: poor in 1945, ad­vanced today.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 48. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jagdish Bhagwati (Johannes Jansson, CC BY 2.5 dk); Sundar Pichai (grapher: Lukasz Kobus (European Commission), CC BY 4.0); Vijay Kelkar (Press Information Bureau, Government of India, GODL-India); Elhanan Helpman (Elhanan Helpman, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: In Defense of Globalization
shelf.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
shelf.why: Ajay’s sin­gle go-to book on glob­al­i­sa­tion, which Amit calls mag­nif­i­cent and the nat­u­ral com­pan­ion to Ajay’s case for it; Bhagwati’s work also un­der­lies the hosts’ ar­gu­ments on rent-seeking.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals
shelf.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored study of out­bound FDI by Indian firms that now build fac­to­ries and com­pa­nies abroad: a glo­ri­ous and often over­looked mode of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion that was unimag­in­able when he was young.

shelf.title: Export Versus FDI with Heterogeneous Firms
shelf.creator: Elhanan Helpman, Mark J Melitz & Stephen R Yeaple
shelf.why: It ad­dresses the ex­port­ing-versus-FDI ques­tion at the heart of the episode.

shelf.title: Exporting & firm performance: Evidence from India
shelf.creator: Apoorva Gupta, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Indian ev­i­dence on the episode’s cen­tral link be­tween ex­port­ing and how well firms per­form.

shelf.title: Export vs FDI in Services
shelf.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored paper tak­ing the ex­port-versus-FDI ques­tion to ser­vices: in Indian soft­ware, firms that in­vest abroad are less pro­duc­tive than pure ex­porters, which turns the stan­dard in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion lad­der up­side down.

shelf.title: India’s Financial Globalisation
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik
shelf.why: Background on for­eign cap­i­tal as a mode of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion.

shelf.title: Motivations for capital controls and their effectiveness
shelf.creator: Radhika Pandey, Gurnain K Pasricha, Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Relevant to his ar­gu­ment that re­strict­ing firms’ ac­cess to for­eign cap­i­tal is as silly as re­strict­ing their ac­cess to im­ported coal.

shelf.title: Did the Indian Capital Controls Work as a Tool of Macroeconomic Policy?
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A closer look at India’s cap­i­tal con­trols, part of the state ma­chin­ery Ajay crit­i­cises for its anti-foreign stance.

shelf.title: Capital account openness in India and a comparison with China: Then versus now
shelf.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora & Rajeswari Sengupta
shelf.why: Shows India’s de facto open­ness to for­eign cap­i­tal ris­ing over the years until India is more open than China: cap­i­tal con­trols don’t close the econ­omy, they just make the rich pay lawyers and ac­coun­tants.

shelf.title: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored paper mea­sur­ing how Indian busi­nesses mis­in­voiced trade on a stag­ger­ing scale to get around ex­change con­trols and achieve de facto con­vert­ibil­ity, which shows that cap­i­tal con­trols fail.

shelf.title: The investment technology of foreign and domestic institutional investors in an emerging market
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Looks at for­eign eq­uity cap­i­tal, one of the modes of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion dis­cussed in the episode.

shelf.title: Foreign Investors under Stress: Evidence from India
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Nirvikar Singh
shelf.why: Examines how for­eign in­vestors be­have in India under stress, rel­e­vant to the for­eign-capital thread.

shelf.title: Foreign Currency Borrowing by Indian Firms: Towards a New Policy Framework
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah & Nirvikar Singh
shelf.why: Connects to his steel-mill ar­gu­ment that Indian firms need cheaper for­eign debt to com­pete glob­ally.

shelf.title: From domestic to global asset pricing
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Part of his kit on what changes when Indian firms and cap­i­tal be­come in­te­grated with the world.

shelf.title: Instant cross-border payments vs. current account inconvertibility
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah & Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
shelf.why: Ajay and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah show that India’s of­fi­cial claim of cur­rent ac­count con­vert­ibil­ity is not true once you read the ac­tual rules and laws, part of Ajay’s case that the Indian state treats cross-border ac­tiv­ity as sus­pect.

shelf.title: Cross-border activities in India need more freedom, not less
shelf.creator: Pratik Datta & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Pratik Datta and Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that the Indian state’s fine-grained con­trol of cross-border cap­i­tal curbs the nat­u­ral free­doms of peo­ple and firms, and that its anti-internationalisation stance needs to go.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Episode 22)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ first episode purely about firms: three com­pa­nies that sur­prised them by how they changed, and why firms, where mod­ern pro­duc­tion hap­pens, are where knowl­edge must flow.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A deep con­ver­sa­tion with Lant Pritchett on why growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion, drives human wel­fare, why causal­ity runs from de­vel­op­ment to ed­u­ca­tion, and why many RCTs solve small mea­sur­able prob­lems in­stead of mov­ing the nee­dle on poverty.

shelf.title: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (Episode 345 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s guests on Bihar de­scribe both the in­ven­tive things hap­pen­ing there, ev­i­dence of India’s un­tapped po­ten­tial, and young peo­ple with­out jobs who have lost hope: the human face of a de­mo­graphic div­i­dend turn­ing into a dis­as­ter.

shelf.title: They Stole a Bridge. They Stole a Pond
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s own piece on the thefts he uses to il­lus­trate India’s raw, mis­di­rected in­ge­nu­ity.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

laughs.text: Amit, dead­pan, on Bihar’s crime wave: “Like an en­tire bridge has been stolen from Bihar. You know, think of the in­no­va­tion. People just stole a bridge... Only in Bihar.” He adds that the bridge went only after a patch of water had al­ready been stolen.

On RCTs: Ajay says you don’t have to be an “RCT Nazi” to study big ques­tions. Amit piles on: “I wouldn’t be sur­prised if there’s an RCT some­where. That do peo­ple per­ceive a yel­low shirt to be brighter than a black shirt? That’s the kind of rub­bish they are doing.”

Amit on Ajay’s per­son­i­fied eco­nomic in­puts: “In a pre­vi­ous episode, gen­tle reader, you met Mr. Gas. Today you have met Mr. Capital.” He says these char­ac­ters re­veal Ajay’s “in­te­rior land­scape”.
Ajay’s sum­mary of what ex­port­ing de­mands of Infosys, since lob­by­ing Delhi can’t win German cus­tomers: “Like shut up and do your god­damn job bet­ter.”
Ajay mock­ing econ­o­mists who treat modes of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion as a menu: “Do I want this, do I not want this? He loves me, he loves me not.”

I18N: Ajay ex­plains that early com­put­ing ran in English on 127 ASCII char­ac­ters. When soft­ware had to sup­port Korean, Japanese and other lan­guages, “com­puter sci­en­tists were very lazy in typ­ing”, so ‘internationalization’ be­came I + 18 let­ters + N.
George Fernandes, whom Ajay de­scribes as “ob­ses­sively ir­ri­tated about multi­na­tional cor­po­ra­tions op­er­at­ing in India”, a stance mod­ern trade the­ory re­jects.
Jagdish Bhagwati, T. N. Srinivasan and Anne Krueger, who drew on India’s fail­ure in the 1960s and 70s to show that ex­port­ing pro­duces a dif­fer­ent, health­ier po­lit­i­cal econ­omy.
Dutch dis­ease: Indian soft­ware ex­ports pushed up the rupee and hurt man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports. Ajay calls it Ricardian trade the­ory at work and “part of life”.
ASML, TSMC and Sony as firms to ad­mire and study: “What is the magic of ASML? What is the magic of TSMC? What is the magic of Sony?”
China under Xi Jinping: global firms re­alised they were over­ex­posed to China and rushed to di­ver­sify. Ajay: “Sadly, not much has hap­pened in terms of Indian gains out of this process.”

Taiwan, South Korea, Israel and Chile, poor in 1945 and ad­vanced today, as the great de­vel­op­ment sto­ries. Ajay notes the OECD hasn’t ad­mit­ted Taiwan, yet it is “a first-class ad­vanced econ­omy”.
Amit bor­rows the idea of ‘fast and fru­gal heuristics’ (one or two sim­ple rules for a com­plex prob­lem) and pro­poses a firm’s level of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion as one.
